To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
HIV-RT binds a specific sequence configuration with a six-base G stretch at the 3’ primer end.
the HIV-RT primer-template binding site is a six base G stretch at the 3´ terminus of the primer.

the SELEX-based method developed here can be used to identify primer-template sequences that are preferred by HIV-RT and that these sequences have a similar sequence configuration to the HIV polypyrimidine tract.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the selection of high affinity primer-template sequences for HIV reverse transcriptase.
the development of a SELEX-based method for identifying primer-template sequences that interact tightly with HIV-RT.
developing an approach to determine the preferred primer-template sequences for HIV reverse transcriptase.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
HIV RT prefers Gs at the 3rd to 6th positions from the 3′ end of the primer.
the G run at the primer terminus was necessary for high affinity binding of HIV-RT.
the G-rich sequence was the optimal primer sequence for binding HIV-RT.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
HIV-RT binds to the polypurine sequence with high affinity.
the polypurine region is a preferred binding site for HIV-RT.
HIV-RT prefers primer-template duplexes that have a 6–10 base run of Gs at the 3’ terminus of the primer, and that these Gs are necessary and sufficient for high affinity binding.
The main takeaway from our work is that
SELEX is a useful method to determine the sequence preference of an enzyme for a particular substrate.
the HIV-RT selection system is robust and can be used to select primer-templates with strong affinity.
HIV-1 RT has a strong preference for primer-templates with a 5′ G-rich sequence.
